banking--how-banks-make-money--t-atm-fee.summary: Out-of-network ATM fees generate billions annually for banks, with the average withdrawal costing over $4.70 in combined fees from both banks involved. These charges disproportionately affect lower-income customers who have fewer free ATM options.
banking--how-banks-make-money--t-atm-fee.whyItMatters: ATM fees are a regressive cost that falls hardest on people who can least afford them. Understanding how these fees work reveals how banking infrastructure monetizes convenience in ways most people do not think about.
takeaways: The average out-of-network ATM fee exceeds $4.70 per transaction
Both the ATM-owning bank and the cardholder's bank charge separate fees
Banks earn over $7 billion annually from ATM surcharges in the US

faq.question: Why do both banks charge for an out-of-network ATM use?
faq.answer: The ATM-owning bank charges a surcharge for providing the machine and cash. Your own bank charges a foreign ATM fee for processing the transaction through another bank's network. Combined, these can exceed $5 per withdrawal.

faq.question: How can you avoid ATM fees?
faq.answer: Use only your bank's network ATMs, choose a bank that reimburses ATM fees, get cash back at retail stores with debit purchases, or switch to a neobank like Schwab or Ally that refunds all ATM fees nationwide.

banking--how-banks-make-money--t-auto-lo.summary: Banks earn billions from auto loans, often paying dealers a markup for steering customers to higher interest rates than they qualify for. This dealer reserve system adds thousands of dollars to the cost of car financing.
banking--how-banks-make-money--t-auto-lo.whyItMatters: Most car buyers do not realize the dealership is profiting by inflating their interest rate. The dealer reserve system creates a hidden cost that falls disproportionately on less financially savvy borrowers.
takeaways: Dealers can mark up bank-approved interest rates by 1-3 percentage points
The dealer keeps the difference between the bank's rate and the customer's rate
Markup disparities have been found across racial demographics

faq.question: How does the dealer markup system work?
faq.answer: A bank might approve you for 5% interest, but the dealer offers 7% and keeps the 2% spread as profit. The bank benefits from a higher-rate loan, and the dealer earns a kickback, while the customer pays thousands more over the loan's life.

faq.question: How can car buyers avoid inflated interest rates?
faq.answer: Get pre-approved for an auto loan from your bank or credit union before visiting the dealership. This gives you a baseline rate to compare against the dealer's offer and eliminates the information asymmetry that dealers exploit.

banking--how-banks-make-money--t-bank-st.summary: Major banks spend tens of billions annually buying back their own stock, returning profits to shareholders by reducing outstanding shares. Critics argue this money should instead strengthen capital buffers or be lent to the economy.
banking--how-banks-make-money--t-bank-st.whyItMatters: Stock buybacks show how banks balance shareholder returns against financial stability. When banks return capital through buybacks instead of building reserves, they choose short-term stock price support over long-term resilience.
takeaways: The six largest US banks spent over $100 billion on buybacks from 2017 to 2019
Buybacks reduce share count, boosting earnings per share even without growth
Regulators require Fed approval before banks can execute large buyback programs

faq.question: Why do banks buy back their own stock?
faq.answer: Buybacks return excess capital to shareholders by reducing outstanding shares, making each remaining share worth more. Bank executives' compensation is often tied to earnings per share, which buybacks directly boost even without profit growth.

faq.question: Are bank buybacks bad for financial stability?
faq.answer: Critics argue every dollar spent on buybacks is a dollar not added to loan loss reserves. If banks had retained buyback capital instead, they would have been better positioned to absorb losses during the 2020 pandemic and 2023 bank stress.

banking--how-banks-make-money--t-credit-.summary: Credit card interest is the single largest revenue source for many banks, with average APRs exceeding 20 percent on revolving balances. Americans pay over $100 billion annually in credit card interest, making it the most profitable bank product.
banking--how-banks-make-money--t-credit-.whyItMatters: Credit card interest rates are among the highest consumers face. Understanding how banks profit from revolving balances reveals why the industry aggressively markets cards and sets minimum payments deceptively low.
takeaways: Average credit card APR exceeds 20 percent, far above other loan types
Americans carry over $1 trillion in revolving credit card debt
Minimum payments are designed to maximize interest collection over time

faq.question: Why are credit card interest rates so much higher than other loans?
faq.answer: Credit cards are unsecured debt with no collateral for the bank to seize if you default. The higher rate compensates for this risk. However, the high rate combined with minimum payments means banks earn far more from cards than their risk justifies.

faq.question: How do minimum payments maximize bank profits?
faq.answer: A minimum payment of 2 percent on a $5,000 balance at 20 percent APR would take over 30 years to repay and cost over $8,000 in interest. Banks set minimums low to keep balances revolving as long as possible.

banking--how-banks-make-money--t-derivat.summary: Banks earn billions trading derivatives, financial contracts whose value derives from underlying assets like interest rates, currencies, and commodities. The global derivatives market exceeds $600 trillion in notional value.
banking--how-banks-make-money--t-derivat.whyItMatters: Derivatives generate enormous profits for banks but also create hidden risks that can threaten the financial system.The 2008 crisis was largely caused by derivatives that spread risk in ways nobody fully understood.
takeaways: The notional value of global derivatives exceeds $600 trillion
The five largest US banks hold over 90 percent of US bank derivatives
Banks earn from the spread between buying and selling derivative contracts

faq.question: How do banks make money from derivatives?
faq.answer: Banks act as dealers, buying derivatives from one client and selling similar ones to another, profiting from the spread. They also earn fees for structuring custom derivative contracts and for providing market-making liquidity.

faq.question: Are derivatives still dangerous after 2008 reforms?
faq.answer: Post-crisis regulations moved most standard derivatives to central clearinghouses and increased capital requirements. However, the market remains enormous and complex, and custom over-the-counter derivatives still carry significant counterparty risk.

banking--how-banks-make-money--t-duratio.summary: Duration risk is the danger that rising interest rates will cause long-term bonds to lose value. Banks holding large portfolios of low-rate bonds accumulated during the zero-rate era faced billions in unrealized losses when rates surged in 2022.
banking--how-banks-make-money--t-duratio.whyItMatters: Duration risk destroyed Silicon Valley Bank and threatened many others in 2023. Understanding it explains how a bank can appear profitable while sitting on massive hidden losses in its bond portfolio.
takeaways: Bonds lose value when interest rates rise; long-term bonds lose the most
US banks held over $600 billion in unrealized bond losses in 2023
Accounting rules allowed banks to hide these losses until bonds were sold

faq.question: How can a bank lose money on government bonds?
faq.answer: If a bank buys a 10-year Treasury paying 1.5% and rates rise to 4.5%, the market value of that bond drops roughly 25%. The bank gets full value at maturity, but if forced to sell early, it realizes a massive loss.

faq.question: Why did banks buy so many low-rate bonds?
faq.answer: During 2020-2021, banks were flooded with deposits from stimulus payments but loan demand was weak. They invested in government bonds for safe returns. When rates rose faster than anyone expected, these safe investments became the source of massive losses.

banking--how-banks-make-money--t-foreign.summary: Banks dominate the $7.5 trillion daily foreign exchange market, profiting from the spread between buying and selling currencies. The largest banks earn billions annually from FX trading, serving corporate clients, investors, and governments.
banking--how-banks-make-money--t-foreign.whyItMatters: Every international transaction involves currency exchange, and banks sit at the center of this flow. The spread they charge affects the cost of global trade, investment, and remittances for billions of people.
takeaways: The forex market trades over $7.5 trillion daily, the world's largest market
The top 10 banks control over 70 percent of FX trading volume
Banks profit from the bid-ask spread on every currency transaction

faq.question: How do banks profit from foreign exchange?
faq.answer: Banks buy currency at one price and sell it slightly higher, keeping the spread. On trillions in daily volume, even tiny spreads generate massive profits. They also earn from advisory services, hedging products, and proprietary positioning.

faq.question: Why do banks dominate the forex market?
faq.answer: Forex trading requires massive capital, sophisticated technology, global client networks, and regulatory licenses. Only the largest banks have all of these, creating natural barriers to entry that concentrate the market among a handful of institutions.

banking--how-banks-make-money--t-foreign.summary: Banks charge foreign transaction fees of 1 to 3 percent on every purchase made abroad or in a foreign currency, generating billions in revenue from travelers and international shoppers who often do not realize the charge exists until reviewing statements.
banking--how-banks-make-money--t-foreign.whyItMatters: Foreign transaction fees are a hidden tax on international activity. For frequent travelers or international shoppers, these fees can add hundreds of dollars annually to the cost of using their own money abroad.
takeaways: Most bank cards charge 1-3 percent on foreign currency transactions
The fee applies to both in-person purchases abroad and online international purchases
Premium travel credit cards often waive foreign transaction fees

faq.question: Why do banks charge foreign transaction fees?
faq.answer: Banks claim the fee covers currency conversion costs and international network processing. In reality, the actual cost is minimal; the fee is primarily a profit center. Visa and Mastercard charge their own smaller assessment, and banks add a markup on top.

faq.question: How can you avoid foreign transaction fees?
faq.answer: Use credit cards that waive foreign transaction fees, such as most travel rewards cards. For debit transactions, Schwab and some neobanks charge no foreign fees. Avoid airport currency exchange kiosks, which charge the highest markups.

banking--how-banks-make-money--t-how-ban.summary: Banks use leverage by lending out many times more money than they hold in capital, amplifying both profits and losses. A bank with $10 billion in capital might hold $100 billion in assets, meaning a 10 percent loss on assets would wipe out all capital.
banking--how-banks-make-money--t-how-ban.whyItMatters: Leverage is why banks are both extremely profitable and extremely fragile. It explains how small asset losses can destroy a bank's capital and why regulators obsess over capital ratios and stress tests.
takeaways: Large banks typically operate with 10:1 to 12:1 leverage ratios
Leverage amplifies returns on equity but also amplifies losses
Pre-2008 investment banks operated at leverage ratios of 30:1 or higher

faq.question: How does leverage make banks profitable?
faq.answer: If a bank earns 1% on $100 billion in assets but has only $10 billion in capital, that 1% return translates to a 10% return on equity. Leverage multiplies modest asset returns into attractive shareholder returns.

faq.question: Why don't regulators require banks to use less leverage?
faq.answer: Higher capital requirements make banks safer but reduce their return on equity and lending capacity. Regulators balance stability against economic output, and banks lobby intensely against capital rules that would reduce their leverage and profitability.

banking--how-banks-make-money--t-how-int.summary: Bank profits are heavily influenced by interest rate levels and the yield curve shape. Rising rates generally boost bank earnings by widening the gap between what they pay depositors and charge borrowers, until rates rise high enough to trigger loan defaults.
banking--how-banks-make-money--t-how-int.whyItMatters: Interest rates are the single most important driver of bank profitability. Understanding this relationship explains why bank stocks rise on rate hikes and why inverted yield curves signal trouble for the banking sector.
takeaways: Banks profit from the spread between deposit rates paid and loan rates earned
A steeper yield curve means higher margins for banks
Rising rates boost income initially but eventually increase loan default risk

faq.question: Why do rising interest rates help bank profits?
faq.answer: Banks can raise loan rates immediately but are slow to increase deposit rates. This expands the spread between what they earn on loans and pay on deposits. Higher rates also increase returns on the bank's investment portfolio.

faq.question: When do rising rates hurt banks?
faq.answer: If rates rise too fast, borrowers default on adjustable-rate loans, bond portfolios lose value, and depositors demand higher rates or flee. The 2023 bank failures showed how rapidly rising rates can destroy banks holding long-term low-rate bonds.

banking--how-banks-make-money--t-how-mor.summary: Mortgages are the largest asset class on most bank balance sheets, generating revenue through origination fees, interest income, servicing fees, and securitization profits. The US mortgage market exceeds $12 trillion in outstanding balances.
banking--how-banks-make-money--t-how-mor.whyItMatters: Mortgages connect banks to the housing market, the largest store of household wealth. How banks profit from mortgages affects home prices, housing affordability, and the financial stability of millions of families.
takeaways: US bank mortgage holdings exceed $12 trillion in outstanding balances
Banks earn from origination fees, interest spreads, and servicing contracts
Securitization allows banks to sell mortgages and earn fees while removing risk

faq.question: How many ways do banks profit from a single mortgage?
faq.answer: Banks earn an origination fee at closing, collect interest over the loan's life, charge servicing fees for managing payments, and can sell the mortgage as a security for an additional gain. Some earn from mortgage insurance requirements as well.

faq.question: Why do banks sell mortgages instead of keeping them?
faq.answer: Selling mortgages frees up capital to make new loans and removes interest rate risk from the balance sheet. The bank still earns origination and servicing fees while passing the long-term credit and rate risk to investors.

banking--how-banks-make-money--t-insuran.summary: Banks generate significant fee revenue by cross-selling insurance, investment products, and protection plans to their existing customer base. This one-stop-shop strategy leverages the trust relationship to sell increasingly more products per customer.
banking--how-banks-make-money--t-insuran.whyItMatters: Cross-selling tactics can blur the line between helpful advice and aggressive product pushing. The Wells Fargo fake accounts scandal was the extreme result of cross-selling pressure taken to illegal extremes.
takeaways: The average profitable bank customer holds three to five products
Cross-selling insurance and investments generates higher margins than basic banking
Wells Fargo's cross-selling scandal revealed the dangers of aggressive targets

faq.question: Why do banks push so many products on customers?
faq.answer: Each additional product increases revenue per customer and reduces the likelihood of them switching banks. A customer with a checking account, credit card, mortgage, and insurance is deeply embedded and far more profitable than a single-product customer.

faq.question: Is cross-selling bad for consumers?
faq.answer: It depends on execution. Genuinely useful product recommendations benefit customers. But aggressive sales targets, as seen at Wells Fargo, can push employees to sell unnecessary products or even create fraudulent accounts to meet quotas.

banking--how-banks-make-money--t-interch.summary: Every time you use a debit or credit card, the merchant pays an interchange fee of 1 to 3 percent to your bank. These invisible charges generate over $100 billion annually and are ultimately paid by consumers through higher retail prices.
banking--how-banks-make-money--t-interch.whyItMatters: Interchange fees are the invisible tax on commerce that funds bank rewards programs. Every consumer pays higher prices to cover these fees, but only cardholders who earn rewards get some value back.
takeaways: US interchange fees exceeded $100 billion in 2023
Credit card interchange is typically 1.5-3 percent per transaction
Merchants pass these costs to all consumers through higher prices

faq.question: Who actually pays interchange fees?
faq.answer: Merchants pay the fee directly but pass the cost to consumers through higher prices. Since prices are the same for cash and card customers, cash users effectively subsidize card rewards programs. This transfer is regressive, benefiting wealthier cardholders.

faq.question: Why are interchange fees so controversial?
faq.answer: Merchants argue fees are too high and set by card networks with monopoly power. Banks argue fees fund fraud protection and rewards programs. Regulators have capped debit interchange but credit card interchange remains largely unregulated in the US.

banking--how-banks-make-money--t-late-pa.summary: Late payment penalties on credit cards, mortgages, and loans generate billions in annual revenue for banks. These fees are designed to be punitive enough to incentivize on-time payment but are often disproportionate to the actual cost banks incur.
banking--how-banks-make-money--t-late-pa.whyItMatters: Late fees hit people hardest when they can least afford them, often compounding financial distress. Understanding that these fees are profit centers rather than cost recovery reveals the economics behind bank penalty structures.
takeaways: Credit card late fees have been as high as $39 per occurrence
The CFPB proposed capping credit card late fees at $8 in 2024
Banks earn over $12 billion annually from credit card late fees alone

faq.question: How much do banks actually earn from late fees?
faq.answer: Banks earned over $12 billion from credit card late fees in a recent year. The actual cost to the bank of processing a late payment is estimated at around $3, meaning the vast majority of the $30-39 fee is pure profit.

faq.question: Will late fee caps reduce bank revenue significantly?
faq.answer: If the CFPB's $8 cap takes effect, banks estimate they would lose $9 billion annually. Banks have argued they would offset this by increasing interest rates and reducing rewards programs, passing the cost back to consumers in other ways.

banking--how-banks-make-money--t-market-.summary: Banks make billions as market makers by standing ready to buy and sell securities, profiting from the bid-ask spread on every transaction. This invisible margin is embedded in every bond, stock, and derivative trade that flows through bank trading desks.
banking--how-banks-make-money--t-market-.whyItMatters: Market making is one of banking's most profitable but least understood activities. The spread on trillions in daily trading volume generates enormous revenue while providing essential liquidity to financial markets.
takeaways: Banks quote both buy and sell prices, profiting from the difference
Market making provides essential liquidity for financial markets to function
The largest banks earn billions annually from market-making operations

faq.question: How do market makers profit from the spread?
faq.answer: A market maker might offer to buy a bond at $99.90 and sell at $100.10. The $0.20 difference is pure profit on each round trip. Across millions of trades and trillions in volume, these small spreads generate billions in annual revenue.

faq.question: Is market making risky for banks?
faq.answer: Market makers hold inventory of securities that can lose value if markets move against them. During volatile periods, spreads widen but inventory risk increases. Banks manage this through hedging and position limits, but losses can be significant during crises.

banking--how-banks-make-money--t-monthly.summary: Monthly maintenance fees on checking and savings accounts generate billions for banks, typically charging $5 to $25 per month for the privilege of holding your money. These fees disproportionately affect low-balance customers who cannot meet waiver thresholds.
banking--how-banks-make-money--t-monthly.whyItMatters: Monthly fees create a poverty tax where the least wealthy customers pay the most for basic banking. Understanding these fees reveals why financial inclusion advocates push for free basic banking services.
takeaways: Average checking account maintenance fees range from $5 to $25 monthly
Fees are typically waived for customers maintaining minimum balances of $1,000-$5,000
Low-income customers disproportionately pay maintenance fees

faq.question: Why do banks charge monthly maintenance fees?
faq.answer: Banks argue that small accounts cost more to maintain than they generate in interest income. Monthly fees ensure these accounts are profitable. In practice, fees often exceed the actual cost of servicing, making them a significant profit center.

faq.question: How can you avoid monthly maintenance fees?
faq.answer: Maintain minimum balance requirements, set up direct deposit, use online-only accounts from neobanks that charge no fees, or switch to a credit union. Many banks waive fees for customers who meet specific activity or balance thresholds.

banking--how-banks-make-money--t-net-int.summary: Net interest margin is the fundamental metric of bank profitability, measuring the difference between what a bank earns on loans and investments versus what it pays depositors. The typical US bank NIM hovers around 3 percent.
banking--how-banks-make-money--t-net-int.whyItMatters: NIM is the core engine of banking profit. Every banking product, strategy, and risk decision ultimately aims to protect or expand this margin, making it the single most important number in understanding bank economics.
takeaways: NIM equals interest earned minus interest paid divided by average earning assets
US bank NIM typically ranges from 2.5 to 3.5 percent
Low interest rate environments compress NIM and hurt bank profitability

faq.question: How does a bank improve its net interest margin?
faq.answer: Banks can improve NIM by raising loan rates, lowering deposit costs, shifting to higher-yielding asset classes, or extending loan durations. In practice, competition limits how much banks can adjust either side unilaterally.

faq.question: Why does NIM matter more than total revenue?
faq.answer: NIM measures profitability per dollar of assets, showing how efficiently a bank converts its balance sheet into income. A bank with massive assets but thin NIM may earn less than a smaller bank with better spread management.

banking--how-banks-make-money--t-overdra.summary: Overdraft fees generated over $30 billion annually at their peak by charging $35 per transaction when accounts went negative. Banks maximized this revenue by reordering transactions to trigger the most possible overdraft charges per day.
banking--how-banks-make-money--t-overdra.whyItMatters: Overdraft fees represent one of banking's most controversial profit centers, extracting money from the customers least able to afford it. Regulatory and competitive pressure has reduced but not eliminated these practices.
takeaways: Banks earned over $30 billion annually from overdraft fees at peak
Transaction reordering maximized the number of overdraft charges per day
A single $5 overdraft could trigger a $35 fee, a 700 percent implicit charge

faq.question: How did transaction reordering increase overdraft fees?
faq.answer: Banks processed the day's largest purchases first, quickly draining the account, then charged $35 for each subsequent small transaction. Five $10 purchases with a $50 balance could trigger four overdraft fees of $35 each, totaling $140.

faq.question: Are overdraft fees declining?
faq.answer: Yes. Regulatory pressure, negative publicity, and neobank competition have reduced industry overdraft revenue. Many large banks have lowered fees, added grace periods, or eliminated overdraft charges entirely. Revenue has dropped from $30 billion to under $10 billion.

banking--how-banks-make-money--t-proprie.summary: Proprietary trading, where banks use their own capital to trade securities for profit, generated billions before the Volcker Rule restricted it after 2008. Banks now operate in the gray area between permitted market-making and prohibited prop trading.
banking--how-banks-make-money--t-proprie.whyItMatters: Proprietary trading was enormously profitable but used depositor-backed capital for speculation. Its restriction changed the risk profile of major banks, though critics argue the Volcker Rule is easily circumvented.
takeaways: Pre-2008 prop trading desks generated billions for banks like Goldman Sachs
The Volcker Rule banned most proprietary trading by deposit-taking banks
Banks argue the line between market-making and prop trading is blurry

faq.question: What is the difference between proprietary trading and market making?
faq.answer: Market making involves buying and selling to serve client needs, holding inventory briefly. Proprietary trading uses the bank's own capital to make directional bets on market movements for the bank's own profit, unrelated to client activity.

faq.question: Has the Volcker Rule actually stopped proprietary trading?
faq.answer: Banks have closed dedicated prop desks, but critics argue that large market-making inventories still allow directional bets that resemble prop trading. The line between permitted activities and banned trading remains difficult for regulators to enforce.

banking--how-banks-make-money--t-selling.summary: Banks monetize customer transaction data by selling aggregated and anonymized insights to marketers, retailers, and data brokers. Your spending patterns reveal lifestyle habits that are valuable to advertisers and marketing companies.
banking--how-banks-make-money--t-selling.whyItMatters: Most bank customers do not realize their transaction data has commercial value beyond banking. Understanding data monetization reveals an often-invisible revenue stream that banks build from your financial activity.
takeaways: Banks sell anonymized transaction data to retailers and marketers
Spending data reveals income levels, shopping habits, and lifestyle choices
Some banks offer opt-out options but few customers know about them

faq.question: What type of data do banks sell?
faq.answer: Banks typically sell aggregated and anonymized data showing spending trends by demographic, location, and merchant category. Individual transaction records are generally not sold directly, but the patterns they reveal about groups of consumers are highly valuable.

faq.question: Can you stop your bank from selling your data?
faq.answer: Federal law requires banks to provide opt-out options for some data sharing. However, many types of aggregated data sharing do not require consent. Reading your bank's privacy notice and opting out of marketing data sharing provides partial protection.

banking--how-banks-make-money--t-small-b.summary: Small business loans generate substantial fee income for banks through origination charges, SBA loan guaranty fees, annual renewal fees, and prepayment penalties that can add 2 to 5 percent to the total cost of borrowing.
banking--how-banks-make-money--t-small-b.whyItMatters: Small businesses are critical to the economy, and the cost of their financing directly affects job creation and growth. High loan fees can make the difference between a small business surviving or failing.
takeaways: Origination fees on small business loans range from 1 to 5 percent
SBA loan fees include guaranty fees of 2-3.5 percent of the guaranteed portion
Annual review and maintenance fees add recurring costs beyond interest

faq.question: What fees do small businesses pay beyond interest?
faq.answer: Beyond interest, businesses face origination fees of 1-5%, annual maintenance fees, packaging fees for SBA loans, appraisal costs, legal fees, and sometimes prepayment penalties. These can add 2-5 percentage points to the effective cost of the loan.

faq.question: Why are small business loan fees higher than consumer loan fees?
faq.answer: Small business loans require more underwriting work, financial analysis, and ongoing monitoring. Default rates are also higher than consumer mortgages. Banks price fees to cover these costs, though the fees also serve as a significant profit center.

banking--how-banks-make-money--t-student.summary: Banks and their affiliated servicers profit from student loan servicing by earning per-borrower monthly fees, late charges, and penalties. The incentive structure rewards minimizing costs per borrower rather than helping borrowers find the cheapest repayment options.
banking--how-banks-make-money--t-student.whyItMatters: Over 43 million Americans carry student debt, and servicer incentives directly affect their financial lives. When servicers profit from confusion rather than clarity, borrowers pay thousands more than necessary.
takeaways: Servicers earn a fixed monthly fee per borrower regardless of service quality
Per-borrower fees create incentives to minimize time spent on each account
Pushing borrowers to forbearance is faster and cheaper than enrolling in income-driven plans

faq.question: How do student loan servicers make money?
faq.answer: Servicers receive a monthly fee per borrower, typically $1-3 for current loans and up to $5 for delinquent accounts. Since the fee is fixed, servicers maximize profit by spending as little time as possible on each borrower, discouraging complex repayment assistance.

faq.question: Why do servicers push forbearance instead of income-driven repayment?
faq.answer: Processing a forbearance request takes minutes while enrolling a borrower in income-driven repayment requires collecting documentation and takes much longer. Since the per-borrower payment is the same regardless, servicers profit more from the quicker option.

banking--how-banks-make-money--t-the-cos.summary: Running a bank involves enormous costs including regulatory compliance, technology infrastructure, branch networks, deposit insurance premiums, and capital reserves. These costs create high barriers to entry and explain why banking is dominated by large institutions.
banking--how-banks-make-money--t-the-cos.whyItMatters: Understanding bank costs explains why fees exist, why banking is concentrated among large players, and why fintech companies try to provide bank-like services without holding a bank charter.
takeaways: Large banks spend over $270 billion annually on regulatory compliance globally
Technology investment is now the largest capital expense for most banks
FDIC deposit insurance premiums cost banks billions annually

faq.question: What are a bank's biggest cost categories?
faq.answer: Technology infrastructure is typically the largest expense, followed by employee compensation, regulatory compliance, branch operations, deposit insurance premiums, and loan loss provisions. Together, these consume roughly 60% of bank revenue.

faq.question: Why is it so expensive to be a regulated bank?
faq.answer: Banks must maintain dedicated compliance teams, file thousands of regulatory reports, undergo regular examinations, hold mandatory capital buffers, and pay into the FDIC insurance fund. These requirements protect the system but create enormous fixed costs.

banking--how-banks-make-money--t-the-rev.summary: Banks profit from employees who move between banking and government regulatory roles, gaining insider knowledge of regulations and building relationships. This revolving door shapes the rules that determine how banks make money.
banking--how-banks-make-money--t-the-rev.whyItMatters: The revolving door creates an inherent conflict where regulators may soften rules knowing they want future bank employment, and ex-regulators help banks navigate rules they once wrote. It shapes the environment bank profits depend on.
takeaways: Former regulators command premium salaries at banks they once oversaw
Banks hire former regulators for their knowledge of enforcement patterns
Cooling-off periods attempt to limit the revolving door but are often short

faq.question: How does the revolving door benefit banks?
faq.answer: Former regulators bring deep knowledge of how their agencies think, what triggers enforcement, and personal relationships with current officials. This inside information helps banks structure activities to maximize profit while staying just within regulatory boundaries.

faq.question: What is regulatory capture?
faq.answer: Regulatory capture occurs when regulators begin serving the interests of the industries they oversee rather than the public. The revolving door contributes to this by creating personal financial incentives for regulators to maintain friendly relationships with banks.

banking--how-banks-make-money--t-underwr.summary: Banks earn billions underwriting initial public offerings and bond issuances, charging fees of 2 to 7 percent for managing the complex process of bringing new securities to market and distributing them to investors.
banking--how-banks-make-money--t-underwr.whyItMatters: Underwriting is how companies raise capital from public markets, and bank fees directly affect the cost of financing. The concentrated market power of a few banks influences how efficiently capital flows through the economy.
takeaways: IPO underwriting fees typically range from 5 to 7 percent of proceeds
Bond underwriting fees are lower, usually 0.5 to 1.5 percent
The top 10 investment banks handle over 70 percent of global underwriting

faq.question: Why are IPO underwriting fees so high?
faq.answer: Banks argue the fee covers extensive due diligence, roadshow costs, regulatory compliance, and the risk of committing to buy shares they might not sell. Critics note that fees have remained at 7% for decades despite technology reducing costs significantly.

faq.question: How do banks choose the IPO price?
faq.answer: Underwriters gauge investor demand through a bookbuilding process, collecting non-binding purchase commitments at various prices. Banks face a conflict of interest: underpricing pleases their investor clients while overpricing pleases the issuing company.

banking--how-banks-make-money--t-wealth-.summary: Banks charge wealthy clients 0.5 to 2 percent annually to manage their investment portfolios, generating billions in steady fee income. Wealth management has become a strategic priority as banks seek revenue less dependent on interest rates.
banking--how-banks-make-money--t-wealth-.whyItMatters: Wealth management fees compound over decades, significantly eroding investment returns. A 1 percent annual fee can consume over 25 percent of total returns over a 30-year investment horizon.
takeaways: Typical advisory fees range from 0.5 to 2 percent of assets annually
A 1 percent fee on $1 million costs $300,000 over 30 years in lost compounding
Banks are growing wealth management as a stable, fee-based revenue source

faq.question: How much do wealth management fees actually cost over a lifetime?
faq.answer: A 1% annual fee on a $1 million portfolio earning 7% costs roughly $300,000 over 30 years in lost compounding. The client pays far more than the simple percentage suggests because the fee reduces the base that future returns compound on.

faq.question: Are bank wealth management fees worth paying?
faq.answer: For simple portfolios, low-cost index funds may deliver better net results. For complex situations involving tax planning, estate strategies, and concentrated stock positions, professional advice can add value that exceeds the fees charged.

banking--how-banks-make-money--t-why-ban.summary: Banks are among the most consistently profitable industries because they borrow at low cost from depositors, lend at higher rates, operate with significant leverage, and benefit from government safety nets that reduce their risk at taxpayer expense.
banking--how-banks-make-money--t-why-ban.whyItMatters: Bank profitability is subsidized by government insurance and central bank backstops. Understanding this reveals that bank profits are partly a transfer from taxpayers who bear the tail risk of bank failures.
takeaways: US banks earned over $260 billion in net income in 2023
Deposit insurance lets banks borrow cheaply because depositors feel safe
Government backstops socialize losses while privatizing profits

faq.question: How does government support make banks more profitable?
faq.answer: Deposit insurance lets banks borrow at nearly risk-free rates since depositors know they will be repaid. Access to Fed lending provides a safety net that reduces funding costs. These implicit guarantees would cost billions if banks had to purchase them privately.

faq.question: Are banks more profitable than other industries?
faq.answer: Banks consistently rank among the most profitable sectors by return on equity. The combination of leverage, cheap deposit funding, fee income, and government safety nets creates a business model that regularly delivers 10-15% returns on equity.

banking--how-banks-make-money--t-why-ban.summary: Checking accounts are the gateway product for banks because they provide cheap funding through deposits that earn near-zero interest, and they create sticky customer relationships that facilitate cross-selling of profitable loan and fee products.
banking--how-banks-make-money--t-why-ban.whyItMatters: Banks compete aggressively for checking accounts because they represent the cheapest source of funding and the strongest customer relationship. A checking account customer is five times more likely to buy additional bank products.
takeaways: Checking deposits pay near-zero interest while the bank earns 4-5 percent lending them
Checking customers are five times more likely to buy additional products
Switching costs keep customers locked in despite better options elsewhere

faq.question: Why do banks offer free checking accounts?
faq.answer: Free checking attracts deposits that fund bank lending at near-zero cost. The bank earns the full interest rate on loans made with those deposits. Free checking also establishes the customer relationship that enables profitable cross-selling of credit cards, loans, and investments.

faq.question: Why is it so hard to switch checking accounts?
faq.answer: Direct deposits, automatic bill payments, and linked debit cards create high switching costs. Changing banks requires updating dozens of payment connections. Banks design this stickiness intentionally to retain customers and the cheap deposits they bring.

banking--how-banks-make-money--t-why-sav.summary: Banks deliberately pay low savings rates because the gap between what they earn on loans and pay on deposits is their primary profit source. Competition for deposits is limited because switching costs keep most customers from chasing better rates.
banking--how-banks-make-money--t-why-sav.whyItMatters: Low savings rates effectively transfer wealth from savers to bank shareholders. When banks pay 0.5 percent on savings while earning 5 percent on loans, the 4.5 point spread is pure profit at the saver's expense.
takeaways: Large banks paid an average of 0.46% on savings while online banks offered 4-5% in 2023
Inertia and switching costs keep most deposits at low-paying institutions
Low savings rates are a deliberate strategy to maximize net interest margin

faq.question: Why do traditional banks pay so much less than online banks?
faq.answer: Traditional banks have branch networks and higher overhead that they fund through wider spreads. They also rely on customer inertia, knowing most depositors will not bother moving money for a better rate. Online banks with lower costs can afford to pay more.

faq.question: Should you move savings to a high-yield account?
faq.answer: On $10,000 in savings, the difference between 0.5% and 5% is $450 per year. High-yield savings accounts at FDIC-insured institutions offer the same safety with dramatically better returns. The biggest barrier is the effort of opening a new account.

banking--how-banks-make-money--t-wire-tr.summary: Banks charge $15 to $50 per wire transfer despite the actual processing cost being minimal. Wire fees are a profitable holdover from an era before instant digital payments, persisting because business customers have few alternatives for large transfers.
banking--how-banks-make-money--t-wire-tr.whyItMatters: Wire transfer fees represent banks monetizing their position as gatekeepers of the payment system. New payment technologies like real-time payments threaten this revenue stream by offering faster, cheaper alternatives.
takeaways: Domestic wire fees range from $15 to $30 and international wires cost $35 to $50
Actual processing costs are estimated at $1 or less per transaction
Real-time payment networks like FedNow are emerging as cheaper alternatives

faq.question: Why are wire transfers so expensive if the cost is minimal?
faq.answer: Wire fees are a legacy profit center. When wires were the only way to move large sums quickly, banks could charge premium prices. The fees persist because business customers need same-day settlement and alternatives have been slow to emerge.

faq.question: Will wire transfer fees eventually disappear?
faq.answer: Real-time payment networks like FedNow and The Clearing House's RTP offer instant transfers at much lower cost. As these networks gain adoption for business payments, wire transfer volume and fees are likely to decline significantly.
